title: Nike Shares Drop 10% on Weak Revenue Outlook, Layoff Plans Revealed by CNBC
body:
Nike’s stock tumbled more than 10 % in early‑trade Friday, extending a second consecutive day of losses after the sports‑wear giant disclosed a weaker‑than‑expected revenue outlook and announced a restructuring plan that includes cutting up to 8 % of its global workforce. The sharp sell‑off sent the company’s market value down by roughly $15 billion, underscoring investor anxiety over slowing growth in key markets and mounting competitive pressure.

The earnings release showed Nike’s fiscal fourth‑quarter revenue slipping 2 % year‑over‑year to $24.5 billion, missing the consensus estimate of $24.9 billion. More troubling for analysts was the company’s forward‑looking guidance, which projected full‑year revenue of $96 billion to $98 billion—well below Wall Street’s median forecast of $99 billion. Management attributed the shortfall to “persistent softness” in the United States and Europe, where consumer spending on discretionary apparel remains constrained by higher inflation and tighter credit conditions.

In response, Nike’s chief executive John Donahoe outlined a “global restructuring” aimed at sharpening the brand’s cost structure and accelerating digital transformation. The plan calls for eliminating up to 8 % of the workforce, roughly 12,000 jobs, across corporate functions, supply‑chain operations, and retail. The company also pledged to consolidate its North‑American distribution network, close underperforming stores, and shift a larger share of inventory to its direct‑to‑consumer (DTC) channels, which have been a bright spot in recent quarters. While the layoffs are expected to generate $1.5 billion in cost savings over the next two years, investors remain wary that the cuts could disrupt momentum in markets that still rely heavily on brick‑and‑mortar presence.

Nike’s challenges are not isolated. The broader athletic‑apparel sector is grappling with a slowdown after a decade of robust growth fueled by “athleisure” trends and pandemic‑era home‑gym spending. Competitors such as Adidas and Puma have already reported modest revenue contractions, and emerging Chinese brands are gaining traction among younger shoppers who favor locally produced, fashion‑forward designs. Moreover, the ongoing trade tensions between the United States and China have added uncertainty to Nike’s supply chain, which depends heavily on manufacturing hubs in Southeast Asia. Recent reports of a slowdown in Chinese consumer confidence—illustrated by a pedestrian scrolling on a smartphone outside a Nike store in Shenzhen on May 31—highlight the difficulty of sustaining demand in the world’s second‑largest economy.

Analysts also flagged the company’s currency exposure as a risk factor. A stronger U.S. dollar erodes the value of overseas sales when they are translated back into dollars, compounding the impact of flat or declining unit volumes. To mitigate this, Nike has been expanding its pricing power through premium product lines and limited‑edition collaborations, but such strategies can only partially offset macro‑economic headwinds. The firm’s recent investment in “Nike Direct,” its e‑commerce and membership platform, has delivered double‑digit growth, yet the initiative still represents a modest share of total revenue and must scale faster to counterbalance weaker wholesale performance.

Looking ahead, the market will be watching how quickly Nike can translate its restructuring blueprint into tangible earnings improvement. The company has set a target of achieving $5 billion in annual DTC sales by 2028, a goal that hinges on expanding its digital ecosystem, enhancing supply‑chain agility, and delivering compelling product innovation. If Nike can successfully navigate the layoffs without eroding brand equity and accelerate its shift toward higher‑margin direct sales, the stock could recover its lost ground. Conversely, prolonged softness in core markets or missteps in execution could keep the shares under pressure. Investors are therefore poised for a cautious wait-and‑see approach as the sportswear titan strives to regain its growth trajectory.
